misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 10. A round trip of 0.1 s fits ten times in a second, so multiply.
That is the window, which is delivered once per round trip, and a second holds ten of those.

questions.prompt: A sender may have 131,072 bytes in flight and the round-trip time is 50 ms. What is the maximum throughput in bits per second?
hints: Find the bytes sent per second first.
There are 20 round trips of 50 ms in a second.
Multiply by 8 bits per byte.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 131,072 bytes per 0.05 s is 2,621,440 bytes per second, and 2,621,440 × 8 = 20,971,520 bits per second.

questions.onCorrect: Halving the round trip doubled the rate for the same window.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in bytes per second. Multiply by 8 for bits.
That allows only 10 round trips each second, but 50 ms fits into a second 20 times.

questions.prompt: A live voice call can tolerate a lost packet but not a late one. Which transport suits it?

choices.label: UDP, because it sends each packet once and does not hold later packets back
TCP, because it retransmits every packet that is lost
TCP, because its handshake keeps the delay low
Either one, because the transport makes no difference to delay

hints: Think about what TCP does with later packets while it waits for a lost one.
A late voice packet is worth nothing.

acceptedIdeas: UDP, because it sends each packet once and does not hold later packets back
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: UDP, because it sends each packet once and does not hold later packets back

questions.onCorrect: A voice packet that arrives late is of no use, so skipping the lost one and playing on gives a short gap instead of a pause.

misconceptions.feedback: TCP delivers the lost packet late, after a timeout and a second try, and holds back everything behind it until it arrives, which is the pause that a voice call cannot afford.
The handshake adds a round trip before any data flows. It does nothing to reduce the delay of the packets that follow.
TCP waits for a lost packet before it delivers the later ones, and UDP does not, so the choice changes how long the listener waits.

questions.prompt: A sender may have 65,536 bytes in flight, and the server is far enough away that the round-trip time is 200 ms. What is the maximum throughput in bits per second?
hints: One window is delivered per round trip.
200 ms is 0.2 s.
Bytes per second times 8 gives bits per second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 65,536 bytes per 0.2 s is 327,680 bytes per second, and 327,680 × 8 = 2,621,440 bits per second.

questions.onCorrect: Doubling the distance halved the rate, which is why paying for a faster link does not speed up a distant download that is window-limited.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate for a 100 ms round trip. A longer round trip delivers one window less often.
That is in bytes per second. Multiply by 8 for bits.

questions.prompt: A TCP segment has sequence number 2000 and carries 750 bytes. What acknowledgement number returns?
hints: Add the data length to the sequence number.
The reply names the next byte expected.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The bytes are numbered 2000 to 2749, so the acknowledgement is 2,000 + 750 = 2,750.

questions.onCorrect: The acknowledgement and the next segment's sequence number are the same number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the last byte received. The acknowledgement names the next one.
That is the amount of data, not a position in the stream.

questions.prompt: A sender may have 16,384 bytes in flight and the round-trip time is 80 ms. What is the maximum throughput in bits per second?
hints: One window is delivered per round trip.
80 ms is 0.08 s.
Divide the window by 0.08, then multiply by 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 16,384 bytes per 0.08 s is 204,800 bytes per second, and 204,800 × 8 = 1,638,400 bits per second.

questions.onCorrect: A small window over a long round trip gives a rate well below what many links could carry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in bytes per second. Multiply by 8 for bits.
That multiplies by 80 in place of dividing by 0.08, which gives a far larger number than a window per round trip allows.

questions.prompt: A client opens a TCP connection to a server with a round-trip time of 80 ms. How many milliseconds pass before the client can start sending data?
hints: The client sends SYN and waits for SYN-ACK.
That is a trip there and back.
The wait lasts as long as the round-trip time you are given.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The handshake of SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK takes one round trip, which is 80 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Every new TCP connection pays this round trip before any data, which is one reason to reuse connections.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts two round trips. The three handshake segments need one round trip in all, because the third goes out as the data begins.
That is the time for one segment to reach the server. The handshake needs the reply to come back too.

questions.prompt: A site has moved to a new address for good. Which status code should its old address return?
hints: Redirection codes begin with 3.
Of the codes that begin with 3, one says the move is permanent.
questions.onCorrect: The 3xx class is for redirection, and 301 is a permanent move, with the new address in the Location header.

misconceptions.feedback: 200 means the request succeeded and the response carries the resource itself. A permanent move has no resource to return at the old address, only a pointer to the new one.
404 means that nothing exists at the URL. A moved resource still exists, and the reply can give its new address in the Location header.
304 says that a copy the client already holds is still current. It is not a redirect and gives no new address.

questions.prompt: Which request header tells a server that hosts many sites which one the client wants?
hints: The server has only the IP address to go on, until the request says more.
The header names the site wanted.
It is the word for the machine that serves a site.
questions.onCorrect: Many sites can share one IP address, and the Host header lets the server tell their requests apart.

questions.prompt: A server replies with the body {"id":7}, which has no newline at the end, and must say in the Content-Length header how long the body is. Which value is correct?

choices.label: 1, counting only the digit 7
3, counting only the letters and digits i, d and 7
6, counting every character except the two braces
8, counting every character, including the braces, the quotes and the colon

hints: Content-Length is the number of bytes in everything after the blank line.
Punctuation is part of the body and is sent like any other character.

acceptedIdeas: 8, counting every character, including the braces, the quotes and the colon
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 8, counting every character, including the braces, the quotes and the colon

questions.onCorrect: The body is eight characters, { " i d " : 7 }, each of them ASCII and so one byte, which makes the header Content-Length: 8.

misconceptions.feedback: Content-Length counts the whole body, which is everything after the blank line exactly as sent, and not only the value inside it.
The braces, the quotes and the colon are part of the body and are sent as bytes, so they count as well.
The opening and closing braces are sent as bytes too, so a body of this kind is counted from the first brace to the last.

questions.prompt: How many bytes is the body {"id":42}?
hints: List the characters one at a time.
Include the braces, the quotes and the colon.
Two digits follow the colon.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The characters are { " i d " : 4 2 }, which is 9, and all are ASCII.

questions.onCorrect: Each character is one byte because all of them are ASCII.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the braces and the colon. Every character of the body counts.
That counts only the value 42.

questions.prompt: What Content-Length is correct for the body {"ok":true}?
hints: Write the body out character by character.
The key ok is 2 letters between quotes.
The value true is 4 letters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The characters are { " o k " : t r u e }, which is 11, all one byte each.

questions.onCorrect: The body is the text after the blank line, exactly as it is sent.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the word true. The whole body counts.
That leaves out the braces. They are part of the body.

questions.prompt: The body {"name":"Zoë"} has 14 characters, and ë takes two bytes in UTF-8. What Content-Length is correct?
hints: Content-Length counts bytes and not characters.
ë is U+00EB, in the two-byte range of UTF-8.
Add one to the character count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Content-Length counts bytes, and the body has 14 characters of which one (ë) takes 2 bytes, so 14 + 1 = 15.

questions.onCorrect: This is the lesson on encodings at work: the header counts bytes, so any non-ASCII character adds to it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts characters. Content-Length counts bytes, and ë takes two.
That gives the ë three bytes. U+00EB is in the two-byte range.

questions.prompt: What Content-Length is correct for the body {"a":1,"b":2}, which has no trailing newline?
hints: List every character.
There are two keys, two values and a comma between.
Each key sits in two quotes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The characters are { " a " : 1 , " b " : 2 }, which is 13, all one byte each.

questions.onCorrect: A trailing newline would add one more byte and change the header.

misconceptions.feedback: That omits the four quotes. Every character of the body counts.
That counts only the letters and digits.

questions.prompt: A request is made for a page that does not exist on the server. Which status code does it normally return?
hints: The class for a request that cannot be satisfied begins with 4.
The code for a missing resource is the best known one.
Four, zero, four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 404 Not Found means the server was reached and has nothing at that URL.

questions.onCorrect: The server is working, which is why a 404 is a 4xx error of the request and not a 5xx.

misconceptions.feedback: That means the server failed while handling a valid request. Here it answered correctly that nothing exists.
That means the request succeeded and a resource is returned.

questions.prompt: After a 301 response, which response header gives the new URL?
hints: The header names a place.
It is in the response and not the request.
The word for where something is.
questions.onCorrect: A browser follows the Location header with a fresh request to the new URL.

questions.prompt: After import hashlib, what does print(len(hashlib.sha256(b"abc").hexdigest())) output?
hints: A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits long.
Each hexadecimal character is 4 bits.
Divide 256 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, and written in hexadecimal at 4 bits per character it is 64 characters.

questions.onCorrect: The length is the same for any input, even an empty one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the digest length in bytes. The hexadecimal string uses two characters for each byte.
That is the digest length in bits. Each hexadecimal character stands for 4 of them.

questions.prompt: A browser trusts a site's certificate because it chains to what?

choices.label: The site's own claim that it is genuine
A root certificate authority the browser already holds
The IP address the page was loaded from
The padlock icon in the address bar

hints: The certificate is signed by an authority, which is in turn signed by another.
The chain has to end at something the browser trusted before it met the site.

acceptedIdeas: A root certificate authority the browser already holds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A root certificate authority the browser already holds

questions.onCorrect: The browser ships with a short list of trusted roots, and a chain is accepted only if it ends at one of them.

misconceptions.feedback: A claim signed by the site itself proves nothing, because anyone can make one. Trust has to come from a party the browser already trusts.
An IP address says where a server is, not who runs it, and it is not part of a certificate chain.
The padlock is the browser's display of the result of the check and not the basis for it.

questions.prompt: After the TCP connection is open, how many round trips does the TLS 1.3 handshake need before the client sends its HTTP request?
hints: The client speaks first and then waits for the server.
Each wait for a reply is a round trip.
Count the replies the client waits for.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The client sends its hello with a key share, the server replies with its certificate, and the client can then send the request: one round trip.

questions.onCorrect: The key share in the first message is what saves the extra round trip that TLS 1.2 needed.

misconceptions.feedback: That was the count for TLS 1.2. In TLS 1.3 the client sends its key share in the first message.
The handshake needs the server's reply, which is at least one round trip.

questions.prompt: The TCP handshake takes one round trip and the TLS 1.3 handshake takes one more. How many round trips pass before the client can send its HTTP request?
hints: TCP needs its own handshake first.
TLS 1.3 needs one more.
Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 round trip for TCP plus 1 for TLS 1.3 makes 2.

questions.onCorrect: The request itself then needs one more round trip for its response.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one of the two handshakes. TLS starts after the TCP connection is open.
That would fit TLS 1.2, which needs two round trips of its own.

questions.prompt: The round-trip time is 60 ms. A connection uses TCP (1 round trip) and TLS 1.2 (2 round trips) before the request is sent. How many ms pass before the request is sent?
hints: Count the round trips of both handshakes.
TCP takes 1 and TLS 1.2 takes 2.
Multiply the total by 60 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1 + 2 = 3 round trips, and 3 × 60 = 180 ms.

questions.onCorrect: With TLS 1.3 the same connection would be ready after 120 ms, which is the gain of the newer version.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only two round trips. TCP adds one to the two of TLS 1.2.
That is one round trip. The two handshakes need three.

questions.prompt: A page is loaded over TLS while someone watches the network between you and the server. What can that observer still see?

choices.label: The IP address you connect to, when you connect, and how much data moves
The page you asked for, but not the address of the server
Nothing at all, because TLS encrypts every part of each packet

hints: Packets must carry an address to be delivered.
TLS encrypts what is inside the packets, and the IP header is outside it.

acceptedIdeas: The IP address you connect to, when you connect, and how much data moves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The IP address you connect to, when you connect, and how much data moves

questions.onCorrect: Encrypted traffic hides what you said and not who you said it to.

misconceptions.feedback: The page you asked for is part of the content, which TLS hides. The packets still need the server's IP address so that routers can deliver them.
TLS encrypts the content of the connection, but the packets still carry addresses for routers to read, and their timing and size can be seen as well.

questions.prompt: After import hashlib, what does print(len(hashlib.sha256(b"hello").digest())) output? The digest method returns raw bytes.
hints: A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits long.
digest() returns raw bytes, not hexadecimal.
Divide 256 by 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, and digest() returns those bytes without the hexadecimal text.

questions.onCorrect: The same input always gives the same 32 bytes, and any change to the input gives a very different 32.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the hexadecimal text. The digest method returns the raw bytes instead.
That is the length in bits. The method returns bytes, eight bits each.

questions.prompt: A server has a round-trip time of 40 ms. A new connection uses TCP and then TLS 1.3. How many ms pass before the client can send its HTTP request?
hints: Count the round trips of both handshakes.
Each handshake is one round trip here.
Multiply by 40 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: TCP takes 1 round trip and TLS 1.3 takes 1, so 2 × 40 = 80 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Connection reuse avoids both handshakes for later requests.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one round trip. TCP and TLS 1.3 take one each.
That counts three round trips, which would be TCP with TLS 1.2.

questions.prompt: What does a hash such as SHA-256 do to its input?

choices.label: It encrypts the input so that the key can later recover it
It turns the input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed
It compresses the input so that it can be restored
It sends the input over a secure channel

hints: A hash always has the same length, whatever the input.
Think about whether a hash value can be turned back into the input.

acceptedIdeas: It turns the input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It turns the input into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed

questions.onCorrect: Because the fingerprint changes if any bit of the input changes, hashes are used to check integrity.

misconceptions.feedback: Encryption can be reversed with a key. A hash has no key and no way back to the input.
Compression keeps all the information so that it can be restored, whereas a hash discards it.
A hash does not carry data anywhere. It only computes a value from the data.

questions.prompt: Light in fibre travels about 200,000 km/s. How many milliseconds does a round trip take over 5,600 km each way?
hints: Divide the distance by the speed to get seconds.
A round trip goes there and back.
Convert seconds to milliseconds by multiplying by 1,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One way is 5,600 / 200,000 = 0.028 s = 28 ms, and the round trip is twice that, 56 ms.

questions.onCorrect: The time depends only on distance and signal speed, so no amount of bandwidth shortens it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the one-way time. A round trip covers the distance twice.
That is the answer in seconds. The question asks for milliseconds.
That is the distance. Divide it by the speed to get a time.

questions.prompt: How many megabits are in 50 megabytes?
hints: A byte has 8 bits.
Convert the bytes to bits, not the other way.
Multiply 50 by 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A byte is 8 bits, so 50 megabytes is 50 × 8 = 400 megabits.

questions.onCorrect: Network rates are quoted in bits per second and file sizes in bytes, so one of them needs converting before dividing.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats megabytes and megabits as the same. A byte is 8 bits.
That divides by 8 where a conversion from bytes to bits multiplies.

questions.prompt: How many seconds does it take to send 20 MB (20 million bytes) over an 80 Mbit/s link, ignoring latency?
hints: Convert megabytes to megabits first.
20 MB is 160 Mbit.
Divide megabits by megabits per second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 MB is 160 Mbit, and 160 / 80 = 2 s.

questions.onCorrect: Doubling the rate would halve the time, as long as the link is the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 20 by 8 and then by 80, mixing the conversions. First convert 20 MB to megabits.
That divides by 0.08. The link carries 80 Mbit each second, so divide megabits by 80.

questions.prompt: What is the bandwidth-delay product in bytes for a 1 Gbit/s link with a 20 ms round trip? One Gbit/s is 1,000,000,000 bits per second.
hints: Multiply the rate by the round-trip time in seconds.
20 ms is 0.02 s.
Divide the bits by 8 for bytes.
questions.onCorrect: A sender needs at least this much unacknowledged data in flight to keep that link full.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer in bits. Divide by 8 to get bytes.
That is the rate. Multiply it by the round-trip time in seconds.

questions.prompt: A 50,000-byte page is sent over a 1 Gbit/s link, which takes 0.4 ms to transmit. The round trip to the server is 56 ms. How many times longer is the round trip than the transmission?
hints: Both times must be in the same unit, and both are in milliseconds.
Divide the round trip by the transmission time.
56 divided by 0.4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 56 / 0.4 = 140, so the round trip is 140 times longer than the time spent sending the bytes.

questions.onCorrect: For a small page the delay is almost all waiting on distance, which a faster link cannot change.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the transmission time. The question asks for the ratio of the two times.
That is the round trip. Divide it by the transmission time.

questions.prompt: A 50,000-byte page is sent over a 1 Gbit/s link, which takes 0.4 ms to transmit, and the round trip to the server is 56 ms. The link is upgraded to 10 Gbit/s. What happens to the time before the page has arrived?

choices.label: It falls to about a tenth, because the link is ten times faster
It falls by about 56 ms, because a faster link shortens the round trip
It barely changes, because most of the time is the round trip and the link only shortens the 0.4 ms

hints: Compare the 0.4 ms of transmission with the 56 ms of round trip.
Which of the two does more bandwidth shorten?

acceptedIdeas: It barely changes, because most of the time is the round trip and the link only shortens the 0.4 ms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It barely changes, because most of the time is the round trip and the link only shortens the 0.4 ms

questions.onCorrect: Transmission falls from 0.4 ms to 0.04 ms while the round trip stays at 56 ms, so a small request gains almost nothing from more bandwidth.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the transmission time shrinks by a factor of ten, and it was 0.4 ms of a total of about 56 ms. The round trip stays the same, so the total changes very little.
The round trip is set by the distance and the speed of the signal, and a wider link does not change either, so the 56 ms is still there.

questions.prompt: Light in fibre travels about 200,000 km/s. How many milliseconds does a round trip take over 8,000 km each way?
hints: Divide the distance by the speed.
Double it for the round trip.
Express the result in milliseconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One way is 8,000 / 200,000 = 0.04 s = 40 ms, and the round trip is 2 × 40 = 80 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Distance alone sets this lower bound, before any routing, queueing or processing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the one-way time. A round trip covers the distance twice.
That doubles the distance but does not divide by the speed.

questions.prompt: How many seconds does it take to send 15 MB (15 million bytes) over a 100 Mbit/s link, ignoring latency?
hints: Convert megabytes to megabits.
15 MB is 120 Mbit.
Divide by the rate in megabits per second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 15 MB is 120 Mbit, and 120 / 100 = 1.2 s.

questions.onCorrect: The link is the limit only while the transfer is long enough for latency not to matter.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the megabytes by the megabits per second. Convert to bits first.
That treats the rate as 10 Mbit/s. The link carries 100 Mbit each second.

questions.prompt: What is the bandwidth-delay product in bytes for 200 Mbit/s and a 40 ms round trip?
hints: Multiply the rate in bits per second by the time in seconds.
40 ms is 0.04 s.
Divide by 8.
questions.onCorrect: A window smaller than this leaves part of the link idle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer in bits. Divide by 8 for bytes.
That is the rate in megabits. Multiply by the time and convert to bytes.

questions.prompt: A browser opens a page for the first time. The resolver answers from its cache in 20 ms, the round trip to the server is 80 ms, and the server takes 30 ms to build the response. The connection needs a TCP handshake and a TLS 1.3 handshake before the request goes out. About how long before the page has arrived?

choices.label: About 290 ms, counting the lookup, both handshakes and the request in turn
About 130 ms, counting only the lookup and the request
About 370 ms, counting TLS as two round trips

hints: The request cannot leave until the connection and its encryption are set up.
TLS 1.3 adds one round trip after the TCP handshake.

acceptedIdeas: About 290 ms, counting the lookup, both handshakes and the request in turn
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 290 ms, counting the lookup, both handshakes and the request in turn

questions.onCorrect: The steps run in order: 20 ms for the lookup, 80 ms each for TCP and TLS 1.3, and 80 + 30 ms for the request and the response, which adds up to 290 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: The request cannot be sent until the connection is ready, so the TCP handshake of 80 ms and the TLS handshake of 80 ms come first and add 160 ms to that total.
TLS 1.3 needs a single round trip after TCP, not two, so the handshakes cost 80 ms each and the total is 20 + 80 + 80 + 80 + 30 = 290 ms.

questions.prompt: In the worked trace the round trip to the server is 50 ms. How many ms does the TLS 1.3 handshake add?
hints: TLS 1.3 needs a single round trip.
Use the round trip to the server.
Take the time as given.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: TLS 1.3 takes one round trip, and a round trip to this server is 50 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the TCP and TLS handshakes costs the same one round trip.

misconceptions.feedback: That is two round trips, which is TLS 1.2. TLS 1.3 needs one.
The handshake needs the server's reply, so it takes at least one round trip.

questions.prompt: The resolver is 30 ms away and the server 100 ms away, with 40 ms of server time. Name lookup, TCP and TLS 1.3 are each answered or completed as before, and the request takes one round trip plus the server time. What is the total in ms?
hints: Name lookup costs the round trip to the resolver.
TCP and TLS each cost one round trip to the server.
The request costs a round trip plus the 40 ms.
questions.onCorrect: The server's own work is the smallest part of the total.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the server time or one round trip. The request takes a full round trip plus 40 ms.
That leaves out the name lookup and one handshake.

questions.prompt: A server is 80 ms away and takes 30 ms to respond. The browser already knows its address and has an open TLS connection to it. How many ms does a second request on that connection take?
hints: The connection is already open.
Which steps are left?
The round trip plus the server time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both handshakes are already done, so only the request remains: 80 + 30 = 110 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Reusing the connection saves 180 ms of every request after the first.

misconceptions.feedback: That repeats the lookup and both handshakes. They are not repeated on an open connection.
That leaves out the 30 ms the server spends producing the response.

questions.prompt: Over HTTP/3, one combined handshake of a single round trip replaces the TCP and TLS handshakes. The resolver answers in 20 ms, the server is 80 ms away and takes 30 ms to respond. How many ms does a first visit take in all?
hints: The two handshakes become one.
The lookup and the request are unchanged.
Add 20, 80 and the request time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 (lookup) + 80 (one handshake) + 80 + 30 (request) = 210 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Combining the handshakes removes one round trip from every first visit.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps two separate handshakes. HTTP/3 combines them in one.
That leaves out the request, which still takes a round trip and the server time.

questions.prompt: A visitor is 160 ms from a server that takes 30 ms to respond. The resolver is 20 ms away, and the connection uses TCP and then TLS 1.3. What is the total, in ms, for a first visit?
hints: Three round trips to the server are now 160 ms each.
The name lookup is still 20 ms.
Add the server time to the request round trip.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the distance more than doubled the time spent on the network, while the server's own 30 ms stayed the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total for the server 80 ms away. Each round trip to the server is now 160 ms.
That leaves out the 30 ms of server time. The request still includes it.

questions.prompt: The resolver answers in 25 ms. The server is 60 ms away, takes 15 ms to respond, and the connection uses TCP and TLS 1.3. What is the total time for a first visit, in ms?
hints: The steps are the lookup, TCP, TLS and the request.
The request is a round trip plus the server time.
Add them in order.
questions.onCorrect: Three of the four steps are round trips to the server.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the HTTP/3 total. Over TCP and TLS 1.3 the two handshakes are separate.
That leaves out one of the handshakes and part of the request.

questions.prompt: With the same figures, a second request on the open connection takes how many ms?
hints: Which steps are skipped on an open connection?
Only the request is left.
A round trip plus the server time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the request remains: 60 + 15 = 75 ms.

questions.onCorrect: The connection's setup cost is paid once and then shared by every later request.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the lookup and both handshakes, which are not repeated.
That leaves out the 15 ms the server spends responding.

questions.prompt: With the same figures, a first visit over HTTP/3 uses a single combined handshake of one round trip to the server. What is the total in ms?
hints: HTTP/3 has one handshake instead of two.
The lookup and the request stay as they are.
Add 25, one round trip and the request time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 25 (lookup) + 60 (one handshake) + 60 + 15 (request) = 160 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Compared with TCP and TLS 1.3, HTTP/3 saves one server round trip, 60 ms here.

misconceptions.feedback: That keeps two handshakes. HTTP/3 uses one.
That leaves out the lookup or part of the request.

flashcards.front: How many different patterns can one byte hold?
flashcards.back: 256, because a byte is eight bits and each bit doubles the count: 2⁸.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 multiplied by itself eight times is 256.

flashcards.front: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit stand for?
flashcards.back: Four, because four bits give 16 patterns and hexadecimal has 16 digits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four bits give 2⁴ = 16 patterns, one per hexadecimal digit.

flashcards.front: Why does the word café take five bytes in UTF-8 although it has four characters?
flashcards.back: The é lies above U+007F, so UTF-8 writes it in two bytes, while c, a and f take one byte each.

flashcards.front: How many clock cycles are there in 1 microsecond on a 2 GHz processor?
flashcards.back: A 2 GHz clock ticks 2,000,000,000 times a second, so a microsecond (a millionth of a second) holds 2,000.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A 2 GHz clock ticks 2,000,000,000 times a second, so a microsecond (a millionth of a second) holds 2,000.

flashcards.front: In the instruction cycle, which step copies the next instruction in from memory?
flashcards.back: Fetch comes first, because the processor must have the instruction in hand before it can decode or execute it.

flashcards.front: Why can a faster clock leave a program no faster?
flashcards.back: A program that waits for memory spends that time waiting however quickly the clock ticks, so the wait only turns into more cycles.

flashcards.front: Roughly how many times longer is a spinning-disk seek (about 10 ms) than a RAM access (about 100 ns)?
flashcards.back: 10 ms is 10,000,000 ns, and that is 100,000 times 100 ns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 ms is 10,000,000 ns, and that is 100,000 times 100 ns.

flashcards.front: Which loses its contents when power stops, RAM or flash? Answer RAM or flash.
flashcards.back: RAM is volatile and loses its contents, whereas flash is persistent and keeps them.

flashcards.front: Why does reading a table row by row usually run faster than column by column when it is stored row by row?
flashcards.back: Each load of neighbouring cells then serves several visits, whereas column order wastes most of each load.

flashcards.front: What is the privileged core of the operating system called?
flashcards.back: The kernel runs in kernel mode and is the only code that touches the hardware directly.

flashcards.front: With 4 KiB pages, how many bits of an address form the offset within a page?
flashcards.back: A page holds 2^12 bytes, so the offset needs 12 bits, which is three hexadecimal digits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A page holds 2^12 bytes, so the offset needs 12 bits, which is three hexadecimal digits.

flashcards.front: Why can one process not read another process's memory?
flashcards.back: Each process has its own virtual addresses, which the kernel maps to different physical frames, so no address of one reaches memory of the other.

flashcards.front: How many bytes of data fit in one Ethernet packet with 20-byte IP and 20-byte TCP headers?
flashcards.back: The headers take 40 of the 1,500 bytes, which leaves 1,460 for data.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The headers take 40 of the 1,500 bytes, which leaves 1,460 for data.

flashcards.front: Name the four layers of the Internet model, starting from the lowest. Type the lowest one.
flashcards.back: The link layer comes first, because it moves frames across a single connection.

flashcards.front: Why is a file sent as many packets and not as one piece?
flashcards.back: Each link carries only a limited number of bytes at a time, and small independent packets let many conversations share a link and let a lost piece be sent again.

flashcards.front: How many addresses are there in a /24 block?
flashcards.back: A /24 leaves 8 host bits, and 2^8 = 256.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A /24 leaves 8 host bits, and 2^8 = 256.

flashcards.front: Which rule decides between two routes that both match a destination? Answer the prefix that is longest or shortest.
flashcards.back: The longest matching prefix is used, because it is the most specific route.

flashcards.front: Why does a longer prefix mean a smaller network?
flashcards.back: A longer prefix fixes more bits as the network part, so fewer bits are left to vary among hosts.

flashcards.front: Which kind of DNS server holds the actual records for a domain?
flashcards.back: The authoritative server for a zone holds its records, and the root and top-level servers only point toward it.

flashcards.front: At which port number does DNS usually run?
flashcards.back: DNS answers questions on port 53, over UDP and, for large answers, TCP.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: DNS answers questions on port 53, over UDP and, for large answers, TCP.

flashcards.front: Why does a change to a DNS record take time to reach everyone?
flashcards.back: Resolvers keep their cached copy until its TTL runs out, so each one learns of the change only when its own copy expires.

flashcards.front: How many round trips does the TCP handshake take before data can flow?
flashcards.back: The SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK exchange takes one round trip.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK exchange takes one round trip.

flashcards.front: Which transport adds only ports and a checksum, with no retransmission?
flashcards.back: UDP leaves ordering and retransmission to the application, which makes it fast and simple.

flashcards.front: Why does a bigger link not always make one download faster?
flashcards.back: A sender can have only a window of data in flight per round trip, so throughput is capped at window divided by round-trip time however fast the link is.

flashcards.front: What is the first digit of a status code that signals a server error?
flashcards.back: Status codes of 500 and above report that the server failed, and 4xx codes report a problem with the request.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Status codes of 500 and above report that the server failed, and 4xx codes report a problem with the request.

flashcards.front: Which header tells a server hosting many sites which one the client wants? Type the header name.
flashcards.back: Host names the site, which lets one server and one IP address serve several of them.

flashcards.front: Why does a 404 not mean that the server is down?
flashcards.back: A 404 is a reply, so the server was running and answered that it has nothing at that URL, whereas a down server gives no reply or a 5xx code.

flashcards.front: How many bits long is a SHA-256 digest?
flashcards.back: SHA-256 always produces 256 bits, which is 32 bytes or 64 hexadecimal characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: SHA-256 always produces 256 bits, which is 32 bytes or 64 hexadecimal characters.

flashcards.front: What signs a site's certificate to say that a key belongs to a name? Type the three-word term for the organisation.
flashcards.back: A certificate authority vouches for the link between a name and a public key by signing the certificate.

flashcards.front: Why does a padlock not mean that a site is honest?
flashcards.back: The padlock says only that the connection reaches the server named in the certificate privately, and a dishonest site can have a valid certificate for its own name.

flashcards.front: About how many kilometres per second does a signal travel in optical fibre?
flashcards.back: Light in fibre travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, roughly 200,000 km/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Light in fibre travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, roughly 200,000 km/s.

flashcards.front: What is bandwidth multiplied by round-trip time called? Answer with its initials.
flashcards.back: The bandwidth-delay product is the amount of data in flight needed to fill the link.

flashcards.front: Why does a faster plan not make a distant website much quicker to start?
flashcards.back: A small request is dominated by round trips, whose length depends on distance, and more bandwidth does not shorten them.

flashcards.front: How many round trips to the server does a first visit over TCP and TLS 1.3 use before the response arrives?
flashcards.back: TCP takes one, TLS 1.3 takes one and the request takes one, so three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: TCP takes one, TLS 1.3 takes one and the request takes one, so three.

flashcards.front: Which transport, built on UDP, combines the transport and encryption handshakes into one round trip? Type its name.
flashcards.back: QUIC runs over UDP and does its own reliability and encryption, so its first connection needs one handshake round trip.

flashcards.front: Why does a second request on an open connection cost less than the first?
flashcards.back: The lookup and both handshakes are already done, so it pays only for the request and the response.
